✧ UNDER THE HOOD

What happens behind one tap

From the 1,231 events in this catalogue to a column of cards on 34 interest paths. This page opens up the five steps in between: how the data is unified, how text becomes vectors, how topics are clustered, how results are ordered, and how it is checked.

Every number here is computed offline by the project's Python code; the page only displays it.

01 Data 02 Vectors 03 Topics 04 Ranking 05 Evaluation
STEP 01 · DATA

Four sources, first made computable

Two sources are open data from data.gov.hk, one is the HKFA fixture page, one is BLAST's organiser and venue pages. Their field names, date formats and category systems all differ, so the first step is not modelling but unification: one ID scheme, one date format, one title key.

Catalogue composition
    De-duplicate by title keyCompare titles after stripping punctuation and spaces, so （音樂會） and (音樂會) count as one group; 1,231 records collapse into 893 title groups, which both the recommendation list and the evaluation rely on.
    Dates: keep only the credibleAn event can span several days and is expanded into a day-by-day list; dates after 2090 are treated as placeholders, removed and flagged so they never sit in "upcoming" forever.
    Missing data: never invent itA missing price is shown as unknown, a missing description stays empty. No generated text is used to "complete" a record, because that would break its provenance.

    Chinese descriptions are missing for 84% of records and prices for 54% — these two numbers explain why the model mostly sees titles, and why character fragments were used instead of word segmentation.

    STEP 02 · TEXT VECTORS

    Turn one title into a 12,000-dimensional sparse vector

    Chinese has no spaces, so each run of Han characters is cut into two- and three-character fragments; English is split into words. Each fragment is weighted by term frequency × inverse document frequency, and the whole record is scaled to unit length — the closer two records are, the smaller the angle between their vectors.

    TERM FREQUENCYtf(t,d) = 1 + ln c(t,d)Take the log: ten occurrences is not ten times as important.
    INVERSE DOCUMENT FREQUENCYidf(t) = ln((1+N)/(1+df(t))) + 1Add-one smoothing: a term in every document keeps weight 1 instead of being zeroed.
    COSINE SIMILARITYcos(x,y) = x · yAfter L2 normalisation the dot product is the cosine of the angle.
    TOKENISATION EXAMPLE
    粵劇折子戲→

    No dictionary is needed; the cost is that 音樂 also appears inside 音樂劇 — a known false match.

    How sparse the matrix is

    1,231 records × 12,000 terms is 14.77 million cells in theory; only 54,000 are non-zero, 0.37%.

    Sparsity means one retrieval is one sparse matrix multiplication; the whole catalogue takes a few MB, so a laptop or a browser handles it easily.

    Schematic at a reduced scale: lit cells are terms with a value.

    This part was cross-checked against scikit-learn: on the same small corpus the hand-written IDF differs from it by at most about 10⁻⁸, which shows the same formula was reproduced rather than "it happens to run".

    STEP 03 · TOPIC STRUCTURE

    Spherical k-means: eight topics

    All vectors sit on the unit sphere, so ordinary k-means would drag its centres off it with a Euclidean mean. The spherical version maximises the mean cosine from each point to its nearest centre; with assignments fixed, the optimal centre is the sum of its members normalised — a direct consequence of Cauchy–Schwarz. Initialisation is a cosine version of k-means++, and three different seeds are run, keeping the best one.

    2D projection (PCA) · each dot is one event · shown only to inspect structure, not used for recommendations

    Click a topic to highlight its dots. Some clusters describe a naming template rather than a semantic theme — for example 51 almost identical dance classes — so these eight clusters remain an analysis layer and are not in the interface; the 34 paths in the product were designed by hand and checked for full coverage.

    STEP 04 · RANKING

    Score with cosine, then remove repetition with MMR

    A user's interest becomes one vector: the query vector plus the average vector of the events they picked, then normalised. The score is the cosine. Sorting only by score usually gives five near-identical programmes, so each pick is penalised by how similar it is to what is already selected.

    MMR = arg max [(1 − λ) · relevance − λ · max cos(candidate, selected)] λ = 0 is pure relevance; λ = 1 is pure novelty; the product uses 0.2.
    Mean similarity inside the listlower means less repetition

    Same query, same candidate set, only λ changes: the mean pairwise cosine inside the list drops from 0.498 to 0.218. Sweeping λ from 0 to 0.5, 0.2 is the point where precision holds and redundancy falls — a judgement, not an optimum.

    STEP 05 · EVALUATION

    With no user data, a catalogue-internal proxy

    The catalogue has no ratings, clicks or ticket records, so supervised learning is impossible. The fallback: sample 100 titles from categories with at least 10 records, exclude the same title group from the candidates, and count how many of the five returned events share the query's category.

    How to read these numbers

    TF-IDF does not beat the keyword baseline on category P@5 (0.610 vs 0.634): the proxy rewards "same category", and the keyword baseline almost always hits when titles repeat literally. The model wins on coverage (0.216 → 0.262) and list diversity (0.383 → 0.333) — for a product that helps people discover, those two are closer to the task; if the task were to find one exact thing, the keyword baseline would be right.

    P@5 always divides by 5: returning a single item still scores 0.2, which prevents "return less to score higher". But it remains a proxy — not user satisfaction, and not an accuracy figure for future data.

    FROM MODEL TO PAGE

    And these numbers became this page

    The model computes the ordering for 34 interest paths offline and exports it as a ~1 MB data.json; the page only handles clicks, filtering and display. So the ranking is auditable, costs nothing at runtime, and the front end and back end cannot disagree.
